opening: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: This case is about whether the State may criminalize truthful speech that merchants believe is their most effective way of communicating the hidden cost of credit cards to their customers. By design, New York's law suppresses the message that you pay more --

I'm sorry. I -- I -- you're two groups of -- of Petitioners. One wants to just give a cash price without any information about the surcharge, and the other, I thought, wanted to give two separate prices. So not everybody doesn't want to give truthful information about the surcharge.

No -- well, they do, Your Honor. They all want to do the same thing. They -- they -- I think what you're referring to is that some of them are doing different things now. One of the Petitioners, Expressions Hair Design, is engaging in dual pricing, they're charging two different prices, one for cash, one for credit, but they are trying as hard as they can to describe that as a -- as a discount so that they comply with the law. The other Petitioners right now are refraining from dual pricing altogether, because they don't want to run the risk of -- of failing to comply with this regime. But if we win this case, all of the Petitioners would like to charge two different prices for cash or for credit, and they would like to be able to characterize the price difference as a surcharge for using a credit card.
That's not what I understood, but your adversary can tell me.
Mr. Gupta, what -- what speech precisely do you think is being restricted?

The -- the message that when you use a credit card, you're paying more, and to be more precise, I think if you look at Joint Appendix 103 through 104, you'll find there the supplemental declaration of Expressions Hair Design where they say exactly what they'd like to do. And if you look at the yellow brief, it's page 1 of the yellow brief, we have a chart. And what we'd like to do, ideally, is describe the pastrami sandwich as $10, and then tell you that it's going to cost a certain percentage more, 2 percent more, to pay with a credit card.
Well, I guess that's why I said like what speech precisely, and you said the message that you're going to pay more if you use a credit card.

But, you know, as -- this -- this statute is not written in terms of speech, it's -- it's written in terms of imposing a surcharge. And -- and let's say that somebody -- let's say that there is a merchant and the merchant charges the list price for something as a dollar and the person comes up to the cash register and offers a dollar bill.
And -- and the cashier says, oh, no. For you it's 95 cents because I impose a surcharge for people who use credit cards; right?
Now, would that violate this law?
I -- you know, I don't know, and what -- part of the difficulty is -- and the reason, we have a vagueness challenge --
You don't know? How would it violate the law?
I don't think -- I don't think it would. I don't think it would. And certainly the State hasn't taken that position --

opinion.title: Opinion Announcement - March 29, 2017
opening: I have the opinion of the Court this morning in Case 15-1391, Expressions Hair Design v. Schneiderman. Each time a customer pays for an item with a credit card, the merchant selling that item must pay a transaction fee to the company that issued the credit card. The petitioners in this case are New York merchants who say that these transaction fees cost them tens of thousands of dollars every year. Now, rather than increase their prices across the board to absorb these costs, the merchants want to pass the fees along only to their customers who choose to use credit cards. Now, there are two ways they could do this. First, they could charge higher prices to credit card users, a credit card surcharge. Or second, they could lower prices to customers who use cash at cash discount. The merchants who brought this case want to use the former approach, imposing a surcharge for credit. They want to do this to make it clear to their customers that they, the merchants, are not the bad guys. It is the credit card companies that are making them pay more, use a credit card, pay a surcharge. New York, however, has a law prohibiting credit card surcharges. The question before us is whether that law unconstitutionally regulates speech. Specifically, what the merchants want to do is post one cash price and then post an additional credit card surcharge, expressed either as a dollars-in-cents additional amount or a percentage increase. For example, Petitioner Expressions Hair Design might wish to post a sign outside its salon reading haircuts $10. We add 3 percent surcharge if you pay by credit card. Or Petitioner Brooklyn Pharmacy and Soda Fountain might list one of the sundaes on its menu as costing $10 with a 30-cent surcharge for credit card users. Now, the litigating parties all agree that New York's law would prohibit them from doing this. The merchants argue that in doing so, New York's law violates the First Amendment. The court that decided this case below, the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit based in New York, ruled that the law did not violate the First Amendment. In fact, that court said that the law didn't implicate the First Amendment at all because it regulated only conduct, not speech. We have said that laws that regulate prices are conduct, not speech, regulations. The law that dictates that all New York delis can charge only $10 for their sandwiches just tells the deli owners how much they can collect each time they sell a sandwich. Now, of course, there will be an effect on speech. The waiters and waitresses can't say that the sandwiches cost something else, and the law regulates what deli owners may say on their signs.
full_text: I have the opinion of the Court this morning in Case 15-1391, Expressions Hair Design v. Schneiderman. Each time a customer pays for an item with a credit card, the merchant selling that item must pay a transaction fee to the company that issued the credit card. The petitioners in this case are New York merchants who say that these transaction fees cost them tens of thousands of dollars every year. Now, rather than increase their prices across the board to absorb these costs, the merchants want to pass the fees along only to their customers who choose to use credit cards. Now, there are two ways they could do this. First, they could charge higher prices to credit card users, a credit card surcharge. Or second, they could lower prices to customers who use cash at cash discount. The merchants who brought this case want to use the former approach, imposing a surcharge for credit. They want to do this to make it clear to their customers that they, the merchants, are not the bad guys. It is the credit card companies that are making them pay more, use a credit card, pay a surcharge. New York, however, has a law prohibiting credit card surcharges. The question before us is whether that law unconstitutionally regulates speech. Specifically, what the merchants want to do is post one cash price and then post an additional credit card surcharge, expressed either as a dollars-in-cents additional amount or a percentage increase. For example, Petitioner Expressions Hair Design might wish to post a sign outside its salon reading haircuts $10. We add 3 percent surcharge if you pay by credit card. Or Petitioner Brooklyn Pharmacy and Soda Fountain might list one of the sundaes on its menu as costing $10 with a 30-cent surcharge for credit card users. Now, the litigating parties all agree that New York's law would prohibit them from doing this. The merchants argue that in doing so, New York's law violates the First Amendment. The court that decided this case below, the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit based in New York, ruled that the law did not violate the First Amendment. In fact, that court said that the law didn't implicate the First Amendment at all because it regulated only conduct, not speech. We have said that laws that regulate prices are conduct, not speech, regulations. The law that dictates that all New York delis can charge only $10 for their sandwiches just tells the deli owners how much they can collect each time they sell a sandwich. Now, of course, there will be an effect on speech. The waiters and waitresses can't say that the sandwiches cost something else, and the law regulates what deli owners may say on their signs. But we have ruled that such an incidental effect on speech does not trigger First Amendment concerns. To cite another example, it is illegal for competitors to fix prices, and they're not protected by the First Amendment simply because they speak to agree on a price. But we think New York's law is different. The law tells merchants nothing about the amount they are allowed to collect from a cash or credit card payer. Sellers are free to charge $10 for cash and $9.70, $10 or $10.30, or any other amount for credit. What the law does regulate is how sellers may communicate their prices. A merchant who wants to charge $10 for cash and $10.30 for credit may not convey that price any way he pleases. He is not free to say $10 with the 3 percent credit card surcharge or $10 plus 30 cents for credit. Instead, if the merchant wishes to price, wishes to post only one sticker price, he must display $10.30 as that price. Because New York's law regulates communication of prices rather than prices themselves, we hold today that the law regulates speech. Because the court below concluded that the law regulated only conduct, not speech, it did not view the law as even triggering First Amendment scrutiny and did not conduct any analysis of whether the law would survive such scrutiny. We generally refrain from deciding questions that the courts below did not consider. As we often say, we are a court of review, not first view. So that means that the court of appeals has some more work to do. We send the case back to that court so it can analyze in the first instance, now that it knows New York's law regulates speech and not just conduct, whether the law is a permissible regulation of speech under the First Amendment. The judgment of the court of appeals for the Second Circuit is vacated and the case is remanded for further proceedings. Justice Breyer has filed an opinion concurring in the judgment. Justice Sotomayor has filed an opinion concurring in the judgment in which Justice Alito has joined.
